title: Ladder Types, Ratings & Selection

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Shop floor. Company ladders lined up against the wall: 6-ft and 8-ft fiberglass stepladders, small and large multi-position ladders, 24-ft and 32-ft fiberglass extension ladders. Danny in front, wide shot.
scenes.says: Job Mindset for ladders. The hazard is a fall, and most ladder falls happen from just six to ten feet. Your first control is choosing the right ladder at the shop, or a lift if a ladder's the wrong tool. Know the ceiling heights before you leave. Plan for the high fixture, the soft ground, the second person for the big ladders. Don't get caught with the wrong size.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny walking the line of ladders, touching each as he names it.
scenes.on_screen: Stepladder - Extension - Multi-position - Platform. No single ladders.
scenes.says: Here's what we use. Stepladders for most indoor fixtures, always fully open with the spreaders locked. Extension ladders for high fixtures, roofs and wall packs, set at 4 to 1. Multi-position ladders for stairwells and odd setups. Platform ladders for long tasks in one spot. We don't use single straight ladders. And a ladder is fall protection only if it's maintained, set up and used properly.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Close-up: a tech reads the side-rail label of the 8-ft stepladder on camera; finger on type, duty rating, material, length. Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Type IA = 300 lb. Includes you, your tools and your materials.
scenes.says: Read the label. Type, duty rating, material, length. Our standard is orange fiberglass, Type IA, rated 300 pounds. Find anything else in the fleet, report it. That rating covers you, your clothes, PPE, tools and materials. A 210-pound tech with a tool belt, a fixture kit and a box of parts is at 240. A 225-pound ladder isn't enough. Ours is.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny between a fiberglass stepladder and an aluminum multi-position ladder.
scenes.on_screen: Fiberglass near anything electrical. No painted ladders.
scenes.says: Material. Fiberglass is required near anything electrical, and keep it clean, because dirt and moisture can make it conduct. Aluminum conducts. Our aluminum multi-position ladders aren't electrically rated, so you always lock out and verify dead first, whatever ladder you're on. Metal ladders are never used around exposed electrical equipment. No wood. And no painted ladders. Paint hides cracks.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: A tech on a 6-ft stepladder under a 10-ft ceiling, standing two steps below the top; graphic arrow showing the top cap and top step crossed out.
scenes.on_screen: Never stand on the top cap or top step. 10-ft ceiling = 6-ft ladder.
scenes.says: Height. Never stand on the top cap or the top step, and on a standard stepladder, not the step right below the cap either unless it's marked as a standing level. Rule of thumb: you can reach about 4 feet above the ladder's height. So a 10-foot ceiling takes a 6-foot ladder. A 12-foot ceiling takes an 8. Stepladders top out at 20 feet by the standard.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Warehouse aisle with a 20-ft high-bay fixture. Danny looks up at it, then gestures toward the van with the extension ladder on the rack.
scenes.on_screen: Too tall? Different access, not a bigger stepladder.
scenes.says: Now a 20-foot warehouse fixture. No stepladder of ours reaches that. The answer is a different means of access, not a bigger stepladder: an extension ladder against solid support, roughly 7 to 10 feet longer than the support point, or a lift if you're trained and authorized, or another plan. If you need both hands for a long time or heavy fixtures, think lift. Ask your supervisor.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Two techs carry the 32-ft extension ladder out the shop door, one at each end, calling "stop" and "turn." Then the large multi-position ladder. Danny voice-over.
scenes.on_screen: Large multi-position + extension over 30 ft = two-person work
scenes.says: The large multi-position ladder and extension ladders over 30 feet, which means every 32-footer we own, are strictly two-person work. To carry, raise and position. Don't try it alone. Most ladder-handling injuries, and a lot of power-line contacts, happen while one person wrestles a long ladder.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.background: Danny at the open van with an extension ladder, 12-ft, 8-ft and 6-ft ladders on the rack.
scenes.says: Our number one ladder infraction is the wrong size ladder. That's why every van carries an extension ladder plus a 12, an 8 and a 6. One of our techs fell off an 8-foot A-frame stretching to reach a photocell it was too short for. Walking back to the van takes two minutes. A fall can take months.

scenes.speaker: Danny Smith
scenes.on_screen: Now read the lesson and take the quiz
scenes.says: Right type, right material, right rating, right height, and two people for the big ones. Now read the lesson and take the quiz.

production_notes: Ladder lineup needs real labels readable in close-up. Two-person carry performed by two techs; keep clear of overhead lines outdoors. The 20-ft fixture scene does not show an extension ladder set up in a warehouse aisle; just the decision. Check that the van ladder set (extension, 12, 8, 6) matches the licensee's fleet before production.
